advances: The proposed integrated reflection comparison holds on the entire assigned two-dimensional decreasing one-resource class, with the explicit absolute constant c=2^-22. In fact the original third depth moment itself is at least 2^-22. Consequently no asymptotic family inside this class can make the proposed ratio tend to zero. The proof uses an actual inner rectangle with its exact mass in the original law, rather than changing the original support or partition function.
author: research-agent
proof:
The set D is finite and contains zero, because both resource coefficients are positive. Hence Z>0. Any closed halfspace containing j includes the closed halfspace with the same nonzero oriented normal and boundary moved to j. Conversely every such halfspace through j contains j. This proves the equivalence in the definition of tau_p. For a fixed j there are finitely many possible subsets of D cut out by these halfspaces, so their finitely many attainable masses have an attained minimum. All tests below use closed inequalities and retain every boundary atom.

Put q_i=e^{theta_i} in (0,1], N_i=floor(R/a_i), and m_i=floor(N_i/2). Define the two integer rectangles
\[
T=\{0,\ldots,N_1\}\times\{0,\ldots,N_2\},\qquad
B=\{0,\ldots,m_1\}\times\{0,\ldots,m_2\}.
\]
Every z in D satisfies z_i<=N_i, so D is contained in T. Also a_i m_i<=a_i N_i/2<=R/2 for each i. Consequently B is contained in the original D. Any point of B that saturates the resource inequality is retained.

For i=1,2 write S_i=sum_{t=0}^{m_i}q_i^t. The remaining indices m_i+1,...,N_i number at most m_i+1. The map t to t-(m_i+1) sends them injectively into 0,...,m_i, and q_i^t<=q_i^{t-(m_i+1)} because q_i<=1. Thus
\[
\sum_{t=0}^{N_i}q_i^t\le2S_i,\qquad
Z\le\sum_{z\in T}q_1^{z_1}q_2^{z_2}\le4S_1S_2.
\]
The original mass of B is therefore
\[
\eta:=p(B)=\frac{S_1S_2}{Z}\ge\frac14.
\]
Let Q_i(t)=q_i^t/S_i on 0,...,m_i, and let Q=Q_1 tensor Q_2 on B, extended by zero outside B. This is only an auxiliary comparison law. On B the exact original probabilities satisfy p_j=eta Q(j); outside B the inequality p_j>=eta Q(j) also holds. The original partition function remains Z.

For each i define a set of integer indices by both closed tails:
\[
C_i=\{t:Q_i(X_i\le t)\ge1/4\text{ and }Q_i(X_i\ge t)\ge1/4\}.
\]
The indices with Q_i(X_i<=t)<1/4 form a prefix. If that prefix is nonempty, its mass is Q_i(X_i<=t_0)<1/4 at its largest member t_0; if it is empty, its mass is zero. Similarly, the indices with Q_i(X_i>=t)<1/4 form a suffix of mass less than 1/4, or an empty set. The union bound gives Q_i(C_i)>=1/2. This argument holds for every finite one-dimensional probability law, including a singleton and laws with a large boundary atom. Independence now yields Q(C_1 times C_2)>=1/4.

Fix j in C_1 times C_2 and a nonzero oriented normal u. If u_i>=0, use the closed tail {z_i>=j_i}; if u_i<0, use the closed tail {z_i<=j_i}. For u_i=0 the chosen tail still has Q_i-mass at least 1/4 and contributes zero to the scalar product. The product of the two chosen tails is contained in {z:u dot (z-j)>=0}, because each summand u_i(z_i-j_i) is nonnegative there. Its Q-mass is at least 1/16. Every closed halfspace containing j therefore has Q-mass at least 1/16. Writing tau_Q for the same closed-halfspace depth under Q, we have
\[
\tau_Q(j)\ge1/16\quad(j\in C_1\times C_2),\qquad
\sum_{j\in B}Q(j)\tau_Q(j)^3\ge\frac14\left(\frac1{16}\right)^3.
\]
The pointwise inequality p>=eta Q gives tau_p(j)>=eta tau_Q(j) for every j in B. Restricting the original moment to B and using p_j=eta Q(j) there proves
\[
\begin{aligned}
M_3(p)
&\ge\sum_{j\in B}\eta Q(j)\bigl(\eta\tau_Q(j)\bigr)^3\\
&\ge\left(\frac14\right)^4\frac14\left(\frac1{16}\right)^3
=2^{-22}.
\end{aligned}
\]
This includes R=0, when D=B={0}, and every case in which one or both coordinate ranges are singletons.

Finally let I_j=D intersect (2j-D). Reflection z to 2j-z is a bijection of I_j. The original log-affine probabilities, with the exact normalization in accepted fact 4121ae9d64b2d14e, satisfy sqrt(p_z p_{2j-z})=p_j for z in I_j. Cauchy--Schwarz therefore gives
\[
\mathsf H_j
=\sum_{z\in I_j}\sqrt{p_zp_{2j-z}}
\le\left(\sum_{z\in I_j}p_z\right)^{1/2}
\left(\sum_{z\in I_j}p_{2j-z}\right)^{1/2}
=p(I_j)\le1.
\]
Consequently \(\sum_j p_j\mathsf H_j^2\le1\). Combining this with the proved lower bound for M_3 establishes the integrated comparison. No numerical enumeration or unattained limiting cap is used: the lower bound applies directly to every containing closed halfspace in every finite member of the class.
statement:
Let a_1,a_2>0, R>=0, and theta_1,theta_2<=0 be finite real numbers. Define
\[
D=\{z\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^2:a_1z_1+a_2z_2\le R\},\qquad
Z=\sum_{z\in D}e^{\theta\cdot z},\qquad
p_j=Z^{-1}e^{\theta\cdot j}.
\]
For every j in D let tau_p(j) be the minimum p-mass of a closed halfspace containing j. Equivalently,
\[
\tau_p(j)=\min_{u\in\mathbb R^2\setminus\{0\}}
\sum_{\substack{z\in D\\u\cdot(z-j)\ge0}}p_z.
\]
Use the original-law notation of accepted fact 4121ae9d64b2d14e with its coordinate dimension equal to two and resource count equal to one:
\[
k_j=\#\bigl(D\cap(2j-D)\bigr),\qquad
\mathsf H_j=k_jp_j,\qquad
M_3(p)=\sum_{j\in D}p_j\tau_p(j)^3.
\]
Then
\[
M_3(p)\ge2^{-22}
\ge2^{-22}\left(\sum_{j\in D}p_j\mathsf H_j^2\right)^{3/2}.
\]
In particular this holds for all positive integer resource coefficients, integer R>=0, and rational q_i=e^{theta_i} in (0,1], as stipulated in the adversarial assignment. The two coordinate dimensions here are auxiliary and do not replace the locked problem's n,d,C,S. This statement does not claim the locked mixed-integer theorem.
